item.title: How long do fruits and vegetables stay fresh?
item.description: Humidity, temperature, light and how long produce has been in storage can all have an affect.
item.content:encoded:
Whether it’s trimming off a piece of mushy parsnip or cutting away a slightly mouldy bit of apple, many of us have used produce long after their peak of freshness.

While fruits and veggies are important for our health, they’re also highly susceptible to bacteria, fungi and other pathogenic microbes. Overripe fruit and veg can harbour E coli, Salmonella and Listeria bacteria, all of which can cause food poisoning. Understanding how to properly store fresh produce can maximise their freshness and keep them safe to eat for longer.

The use-by dates printed on packaging are usually a useful indicator of how long fresh produce can safely be stored and eaten. But the environment fresh produce is stored in can affect the shelf-life of produce – so use-by dates may not always be accurate.

Fruit and veg are living – so things like humidity, temperature, atmospheric gas, light, how long it’s been in storage and any potential microbial contamination can all affect how long produce can be stored.

The ideal storage conditions will also be different for each fruit and vegetable.

Fruit

Apples have a shelf-life of around one week at room temperature, and three to four weeks in the fridge. These should ideally be stored in the fridge’s veg drawer and washed before eating.

item.title: Madras HC strikes down order giving government jobs to kin of Karur stampede victims
item.description: The bench said that such actions were not appropriate when there was a waiting list for appointments to public jobs on compassionate grounds.
item.content:encoded:
The Madurai bench of the Madras High Court on Monday struck down a Tamil Nadu government order granting government jobs on compassionate grounds to the family members of the persons who died in the Karur stampede, Live Law reported.

The stampede took place on September 27 at Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam chief Vijay’s rally in Karur district when he was addressing supporters from his campaign vehicle. Forty-one persons had died in the stampede.

Vijay went on to become the chief minister of Tamil Nadu on May 10 after his party became the single-largest party in the Assembly elections.

A division bench of Justices CV Karthikeyan and R Sakthivel held that the appointments of the family members of the victims of the stampede violated constitutional provisions pertaining to the right to equality and the right to equal opportunity in matters of public employment.

The bench observed that many people were waiting for compassionate appointments in government departments.

“When there is a waiting list, it is not appropriate to overlook their needs and extend what is termed as succor to family members of the Karur incident,” Live Law quoted the court as saying.

item.title: India’s mega textile parks are yet to take off but the Centre plans to build more
item.description: The sector can boost industrial capacity and create jobs, however government audits show the 20-year-old scheme is flailing.
item.content:encoded:
The Indian government has proposed to set up mega textile parks in challenge mode, even as similar programmes have, in the past, failed to meet their investment and employment generation targets.

India’s textiles sector contributes to 2.3% of the gross domestic product and with 45 million direct workers, is the country’s second largest employer, after agriculture. About 80% of its capacity lies in micro, small and medium enterprises.

When unveiling the 2026-’27 budget earlier this year, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman proposed setting up mega textile parks in challenge mode. But she had made a similar announcement five years ago at the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic, for setting up seven textile parks with a three-year timeline.

In March, the government told the Lok Sabha that it has finalised seven textile parks under Pradhan Mantri Mega Integrated Textile Region and Apparel. Today, approach roads are being constructed in three of the proposed parks: in Dhar (Madhya Pradesh), Warangal (Telangana), and Kalaburgi (Karnataka), while two parks in Virudhunagar (Tamil Nadu) and Amravati (Maharashtra) are inviting potential allottees.

Two others, in Navsari (Gujarat) and in Lucknow (Uttar Pradesh), saw their bid documents being approved by the Public Private Partnership Appraisal Committee. The attack took place when the vessel, MV OMORFI, was reportedly transiting through Russian territorial waters in the Black Sea, the ministry said on Friday.

The ministry said that it conveyed its “serious concern” about the attack to Ukrainian ambassador Oleksandr Polishchuk and condemned attacks on commercial shipping.

item.title: ‘To mark my home within the luminescence of poetry’: Poems from a new book on the self in the city
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Absurd Theatre’, by Suchita Parikh-Mundul.
item.content:encoded:
To own a home

To own a home is to ingest it
and hope the concrete doesn’t
reverse track. It is to pray
the apartment breaks
down into paste in the entrails —
a process that takes as long
as final possession. It is to serve
the carpet area with a side of dadi’s
pickle (which the broker enjoys)
while the builder consumes seventy per cent
in cash, deep fried, and the rest
via bank transfer. (No salad.)

It is to feel lime-washed walls
slide down the throat with deceptive
sweetness and swirl in the abdomen
along with years of EMIs.
It is to brace for the acidity
of loan interests, corrosion of the inner
lining, lacerations and leakage.

It is to tackle complaints from neighbours,
which involves too much caffeine.
It is to watch the ceiling
peel, which is nobody’s concern
but yours. It is to devour meals
on the sly like a sleep-eater.
It is to decorate each room with care
and diabetic sugar, hoping everything
dissolves easily into bile. It is to feel
as if you have swallowed a rock,
though others are quick
to assure you this is normal
for property ownership and crucial
for a comfortable life.


Coastal road

The coastal road curves above the diamonds
of the Arabian Sea like an armful of edelweiss.
We drive towards its hologram
of urbanity, watching it expand like a promise,
noting how it links dreams to the soul.

item.title: Centre introduces new anti-paper leak bill in Lok Sabha after nationwide protests
item.description: The draft legislation proposes imprisonment of five to ten years and a fine of up to Rs 50 lakh for those found using unfair means in public examinations.
item.content:encoded:
The Union government on Monday introduced a bill to amend the anti-paper leak law in the wake of nationwide protests against alleged irregularities in competitive examinations.

The 2026 Public Examinations Prevention of Unfair Means Amendment Bill was introduced by Union minister Jitendra Singh as Opposition MPs shouted slogans criticising the police for using excessive force against protesters in Delhi on July 20.

Subsequently, the House was adjourned till 5 pm.

What does the bill say?

The legislation proposes imprisonment of five to ten years for individuals found using unfair means in public examinations. The maximum fine for such persons would increase from Rs 10 lakh to Rs 50 lakh.

If instances of paper leaks or other offences listed under the bill are found to be organised, the bill proposes a minimum sentence of seven years and a fine of up to Rs 10 crore.

A total of 15 illegal acts, including leaking question papers, tampering with optical mark recognition sheets, creating fake websites and issuing fake admit cards, have been listed as offences under the bill, reported The Indian Express.

Optical Mark Recognition is a system that reads answers marked by candidates by detecting filled bubbles or marks on an answer sheet.

item.title: Frugal, uncomplicated: What former PM Charan Singh’s meals were like (and a recipe from his kitchen)
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Prime Minister’s Table: Delicacies and Diplomacies from the Era of Nehru to Modi’, by Purabi Shridhar and Sanghita Singh.
item.content:encoded:
Charan Singh was a frugal eater and a strict vegetarian. According to Ajit Singh, his son, “He had no interest in food. His regular meals would be dal, roti and one vegetable. I don’t think there were any accompaniments, and he would never eat more than one, or, at best, two rotis. Also, where was that much money to cook several dishes for so many people?” For breakfast, however, Charan Singh would generally have alu ka paratha. Ajit Singh also remembered that at one time there was a family cook called Chintamani who “would make great cheela (gram flour pancake) and he used to have it for breakfast.”

The former prime minister preferred it with lemon pickle or asafoetida-mango pickle. Sudhir Varma echoed what his uncle said, “In general, his eating habits were very frugal, simple and the food cooked in our kitchen was also very basic. Nothing exotic here, nor did it entail any complicated recipe.” According to Sudhir Verma, his grandfather’s breakfast, apart from the special tea he would have, comprised “some dry fruits and maybe some Isabgol husk. A guava fruit was also added sometimes, plucked from the trees in our house. And every once in a while, he would have cheela.”

item.title: Opinion: The Modi government doesn’t understand Gen Z’s protest memes – but that doesn’t matter

Another claimed that the protester’s ex had ignored them less than the government had. In Bengaluru, pop singer Taylor Swift appeared on a sign to note that theIndian exam papers had leaked– but photographs of her recent wedding had not.

item.title: This book asks if unemployment often translates to cynicism and desire for strong-armed leadership
item.description: An excerpt from ‘To Kill a Democracy: India’s Passage to Despotism’, by Debasish Roy Chowdhury and John Keane.
item.content:encoded:
The dangerous work environment of Indian workers is symptomatic of the global decline of organised labour and the corresponding rise of what’s now widely called the “precariat”. India’s new slavery is an egregious version of this trend. A global class of labour that lives perpetually in economic uncertainty and moves in and out of jobs that give little meaning to their lives, the precariat are characterised by volatile earnings, chronic debt, and a lack of non-wage and rights-based state benefits.

In the global hierarchy of labour, they come below the traditional working class, for whom welfare states were built and trade unions acted. In India, where welfare provisions are poor and more than 90% of workers are in the informal sector, the social foundations of working life have historically been degraded. The shrinking space for unionisation has further degraded social life and working conditions. Like elsewhere, the power of organised industrial workers, among the most potent modern agents of social dignity and democratisation, has been systematically eroded in India.

item.title: India’s lost generation: Education was a secure investment, now it’s a gamble
item.description: The destruction of public education has forced students to rely on an expensive and exploitative private sector while there is no guarantee of jobs.
item.content:encoded:
A stark and urgent crisis has been unfolding in Indian society over the years. The dream of education as a guaranteed path to upward mobility has been crumbling. The “GenZ” protests we are witnessing in India today has brought the crisis into sharp relief but millions of families have long been suffering its consequences. Some of the aspects of the problem are still not fully acknowledged in public discourse.

For generations, Indian families have treated education as the surest ticket to upward mobility. Even the poor scraped together whatever they could, sometimes at devastating personal cost, in the belief that a degree would lift their children, and therefore the family, into the economic stability and respectability of the middle class.

Education was an investment strategy, a form of social insurance and a retirement plan for parents who sacrificed everything for their children’s success.

However, recent trends indicate that the privatisation of education, rising costs of coaching and a shrinking job market have disrupted this conventional wisdom.

The gamble

item.title: Can you pay off your ‘sleep debt’?
item.description: Studying the effects of short sleep shows that biological systems are more dynamic and adaptable.
item.content:encoded:
Maybe you’re a new parent or someone who lies awake at night. If so, you may have started to worry you’re not getting enough sleep.

Sleep wearables don’t help. They can show your “sleep debt”, a running total of how far you’ve fallen behind.

But the word “debt” assumes your sleep works like a bank account. It assumes lost hours stack up, carry over, and you must eventually repay them in full.

But sleep doesn’t really work this way. And chasing “enough sleep” may not be helping.

What is a sleep debt?

item.title: Greek-Roman philosopher Plutarch’s ancient advice for how to be happier online
item.description: How to avoid being triggered by others’ provocations and how to benefit from disagreement.
item.content:encoded:
For many centuries, the writings of Plutarch of Chaeronia (c.46-119CE) were at the heart of elite humanistic education in the West. We can see the influence of his Lives of Eminent Greeks and Romans and the philosophical essays in his work Moralia in early modern authors from Michel de Montaigne and Francis Bacon to William Shakespeare.

Many of Plutarch’s essays also have a practical focus that can seem very timely in our social media age. He writes about how to cool the desire to gossip and pry into other people’s lives and how not to be taken in by salacious stories.

He gives advice about how to avoid being triggered by others’ provocations and how to benefit from disagreement. He advises on how to speak about ourselves without boasting or self-advertisement, how to tell friends from conmen (or flatterers) trying to sell us something, and how to pay attention so our minds are not overloaded and scattered.

It almost seems as if Plutarch was peering into the 21st century and responding to the mental health challenges our commercialised social media is producing at scale.

The reality, as journalist Max Fisher outlines in his book The Chaos Machine, is that social media companies have identified the same psychological vulnerabilities Plutarch hoped to help readers to correct, recognising them as effective ways to “maximise user engagement”.

Another change of guard in Downing Street has triggered a renewed bout of concern – and sniggers – over the fragility of British politics and its democracy. Not for the first time, as the country gets its seventh prime minister in 10 years. item.title: ‘Daddy, detain me’: The memes that humbled Modi
item.description: When chronically online youth took to the streets, they stripped the state’s harshest response of the fear it was meant to inspire.

The Cockroach Janta Party was born as an Instagram page on May 16, when Abhijeet Dipke asked unemployed young people of the country, who the Chief Justice of India had dubbed “cockroaches”, to come together.

Its mascot was an AI-generated cockroach in sunglasses.

From that moment on, tens of thousands of young people rallied behind what was, in essence, an AI-slop Instagram page, and joined protests across the country.

The movement intensified after activist Sonam Wangchuk was forcibly removed from Jantar Mantar on the 21st day of his hunger strike, and when the police cracked down on their march towards Parliament with lathi charges, tear gas and pellet guns.

The young protestors responded to the violence – with memes and irreverence.

This was not a movement trying to imitate the student politics of the 1990s. It spoke the language of the internet because that was where much of its constituency already lived.

And so began the meme offensive.

Subway Surfers or lathi charge?

Take the “Everybody knows that I'm a good girl, officer” trend. The audio comes from Playing Dangerous, an unreleased 2012 Lana Del Rey song in which she playfully insists on her innocence to a police officer. item.title: How Mughal emperors embraced a syncretic sartorial sensibility
item.description: From self-expression to diplomatic posturing, Indic dress codes and textiles permeated their clothing choices.
item.content:encoded:
In his memoirs, the Tuzuk-i Jahangiri, Jahangir is represented as the quintessential aesthete. This is exemplified in his miniature portraits, often featuring a host of luxurious objects, such as jade wine cups, jewel-encrusted daggers, and finely woven textiles.

In one such painting, where he is depicted in his typical resplendent regalia, two overlapping textile sashes or patkas gracefully wind around his torso – one bearing a distinctive bandhani tie-dye design, emblematic of Rajputana culture, and the other displaying intricate Islamicate geometric designs.

These twin sashes depict a carefully crafted visual manifesto of the emperor’s filial identity – as the son of both his Muslim father, the Mughal emperor Akbar, and Hindu mother, Rajput princess Harkha Bai.

This kind of multicultural sartorial sensibility reached refined heights during the reign of Akbar and his successors but did not originate in Mughal courts. Art historian Finbarr Barry Flood in his book Objects of Translation argues that between the 10th and 12th centuries, medieval elites engaged in “cultural cross-dressing” at cosmopolitan zones of contact around mercantile hubs in northern India.

Muslim elites adopted luxury items of ornamentation and dress favoured by rich Hindu and Buddhist rulers while Buddhist and Hindu elites reciprocally took to “fashionable” Turko-Persian wear as a sign of their sophisticated, worldly tastes. Such exchanges...

item.title: ‘A Critical History of Kannada Literature’: A much-needed history of a major literary culture
item.description: Author Rajendra Chenni offers a critical history of Kannada literature, tracing its development from ancient texts to contemporary writing.
item.content:encoded:
Rajendra Chenni’s A Critical History of Kannada Literature is a timely, much-needed, readable history of one of India’s major literary cultures. While there have been such overviews before, it is necessary that each generation rewrite history with new foci and commitments. It is increasingly rare – in the age of academic specialisations – for scholars to be able to summon up a millennium and a half of literary production and be able to engage in good-faith conversation and dialogue with that tradition.

Chenni begins with some of the unavoidable issues of literary historiography. The first canonical text, the 9th-century Kavirajamarga, is celebrated as arguably the “first book of aesthetics in a vernacular language anywhere in the world”. Unsurprisingly, however, the content is deeply indebted to the Sanskrit tradition of scholars such as Bhamaha and Dandin.

The beginnings

What one thus needs is an appreciation of more reflective, rather than reflexive, nationalisms and sub-nationalisms. Further, the Kavirajamarga has a seemingly unproblematic engagement with worldly authority – it pits itself against other regional polities, but does not question aesthetics itself as needing to be homogenised and entirely aligned with political power.

item.title: Why you keep buying books you don’t read – and why it feels so good
item.description: Looking forward to enjoyable experiences, such as reading a new book, can improve mood, increase motivation and provide a buffer against everyday stress.
item.content:encoded:
At busy times, I find I simply cannot read as much as I would like to. Life has a habit of filling every available hour with work, meetings, emails, chores, errands and deadlines. Standing in one of my natural habitats – a bookshop – it is frustrating to see so many things I want to read while knowing I do not have the time.

My usual consolation is to buy the book anyway and let a small, satisfying pile build up, looking ahead to the next quieter stretch when I might finally open them. It is oddly satisfying. Some might call this clutter. The Japanese have a far more elegant word for it: tsundoku.

The term describes the habit of acquiring books and allowing them to accumulate unread. It combines the idea of stacking things up (tsunde), leaving something for later (oku) and reading (doku). The result is a concept that captures the quiet optimism of a pile of books.

Far from being a sign of being time poor or lacking in discipline, tsundoku may reveal something surprisingly important about how the brain responds to anticipation.

item.title: ‘Whistler’ by Ann Patchett: A luminous story of loving the family beyond one’s capacity

item.content:encoded:
Ann Patchett’s Whistler opens with its protagonist, 53-year-old Daphne Zabriskie, running into her former stepfather on a random Friday. It’s a loaded encounter. Daphne bursts into tears, and Eddie Triplett – the stepfather in question – decides he needs a drink before noon. But it means that over 40 years later, their lives are connected again – a reality that they spend the rest of the time settling into.

Eddie is one of three fathers to Daphne and her sister, Leda: their late biological father left them to live on his sailboat full-time, and their mother’s current husband is cordial but has a family of his own. item.title: ‘Ode to a Grieving Angel’: Naveen Kishore’s poems on the genesis of art muse about its afterlife
item.description: Kishore returns to his preoccupation with silence – themes that were central to his previous collections, ‘Mother Muse Quintet’ and ‘Knotted Grief.’
item.content:encoded:
In his third collection of poems, Ode to a Grieving Angel, poet Naveen Kishore returns as a theatre-lighting designer, his poems a witness to the artistic process.

A purgatory of suffering

The first section, also the longest, unfurls on the stage with the poet witnessing the play of light and shadow from the wings. Like the actors, the reader too is caught in the “glare of spotlights” while Shakespeare’s iconic plays are performed in a rather grotesque manner. The darkness of the shadows is juxtaposed with a “barren” stage and colourless trees, the actors a zombie version of themselves. Characters from Macbeth, Hamlet, and King Lear find themselves together on the same stage, jostling for space, tripping over wires, and burning in fading light. The audience has disappeared into the dark and the actors are a heap of anxiety and confusion. For Kishore, Shakespeare’s heroes and heroines are pitiful – with a limited vocabulary and appearances, they are doomed to repeat their fates over and over again. Unlike the audience, they may not exit into the light. Not yet. The stage, despite its careful choreography, is a purgatory of suffering.

item.title: When Ranjit Singh wanted to send the Koh-i-noor to Jagannath: An English artist writes
item.description: Emily Eden’s writings and paintings offer insights into interactions between Sikhs and the British a decade before their annexation of Punjab.
item.content:encoded:
In the late 1830s, in north India, the artist and writer Emily Eden was fascinated by Sikhs – both royalty and commoners. She visited Sikh religious sites and experienced the hospitality of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

Emily and her younger sister Frances (Fanny) accompanied their brother George, Lord Auckland, India’s newly appointed governor-general, on his progress across north India, from October 1837 to December 1838. Occasional mentions of Sikhs continue to appear in her correspondence till at least November 1839.

When Lord Auckland and his sisters met Ranjit Singh in December 1838, they probably knew little of the Sikhs’ distinctive religious and martial heritage.

Luckily there were interpreters, and Emily had a sharp intellect, acute powers of observation, liberal Whig values and a lively curiosity about people. She also had a keen sense of humour. She journalled and painted assiduously and prolifically.

Among nineteenth-century Western sources on Sikh history, historians have usually drawn on the more formal accounts published by male authors. The journals and letters of women, as well as their sketches and paintings, have been largely overlooked. So, consideration is overdue of Emily Eden’s insights into interactions between Sikhs and the British a decade before their annexation of Punjab.

item.title: ‘Open Intelligence’: An eye-opening account of the future of creative arts in the age of AI
item.description: Saikat Majumdar’s book compels readers to reflect on the unique distinction between a human student and an AI student of the creative arts.
item.content:encoded:
In one of the early chapters of his latest book, Open Intelligence: Education Between Art and Artificial, Saikat Majumdar establishes his thesis argument: Art and artifice shape each other, and hence, in the end, remain inseparable. He further responds to the age-old debatable question of whether creative arts can be taught with distinguished clarity. Majumdar elucidates that “all art has a dimension that is more like science…art forms with more visible scientific patterns have more teachable components…It has been easy for AI to pick up the scientific, learnable patterns and technical foundations of all art forms.”

item.title: Youth protests: Why India’s streets have become the new floor of the House
item.description: A parliament that does not adequately represent disagreement cannot expect citizens to confine their democratic frustrations within its walls.
item.content:encoded:
Every democracy has two arenas of politics. One is formal: legislatures, courts, committees, elections and party offices. The other is informal – streets, campuses, public meetings and citizens’ movements. The health of a democracy depends on the relationship between these two spaces.

In a functioning republic, parliament absorbs public anxieties and converts them into debate, legislation and accountability. Movements outside parliament push institutions when they become complacent. The two are part of the same democratic ecosystem.

India’s present crisis lies in the weakening of that relationship.

Social scientist and activist Yogendra Yadav recently argued that the Opposition must stop viewing elections as the beginning and end of politics and rediscover the tradition of democratic resistance. It is an argument with deep roots in Indian political history.

The freedom movement was not a parliamentary exercise. The movements against the Emergency were not conducted through legislative procedure. Many of India’s most significant democratic gains came when citizens stepped outside formal institutions and demanded that those institutions live up to their constitutional promises.

The question before the Opposition today is whether it can recover that political imagination.

item.title: Weight-loss injections could set off new kind of ‘yo-yo dieting’
item.description: Medication such as Wegovy and Mounjaro should be best understood as a window of opportunity to build long-term habits.
item.content:encoded:
For many people living with obesity, newer weight-loss medicines such as Wegovy and Mounjaro have been transformative. These drugs are often grouped under the label GLP-1 medicines because they mimic hormones released after eating, helping people feel fuller and less hungry. Mounjaro, whose active ingredient is tirzepatide, also acts on another hormone involved in appetite and blood sugar control.

At a time when more than 1 billion people worldwide are living with obesity, these medicines are widely viewed as among the biggest advances in obesity treatment. But one important question is becoming harder to avoid: what happens when people stop taking them?

Evidence points to an uncomfortable answer. Many people regain a significant amount of the weight they have lost. A recent study found that, after people stopped weight-loss medications, weight and several heart health markers tended to move back towards pre-treatment levels over time. Other studies have found similar patterns after stopping semaglutide and tirzepatide.

This makes biological sense. These medicines work partly by reducing appetite and increasing feelings of fullness. People often describe this as a reduction in “food noise”, meaning the intrusive thoughts, cravings or urges around eating that can make it difficult to eat less. item.title: As El Niño grows stronger, India may have to rely more on coal energy
item.description: Hydropower generation has declined due warmer weather and lower rainfall so far.
item.content:encoded:
Amidst a rise in electricity demand driven by warmer conditions in June, hydropower generation has declined, increasing India’s reliance on coal-fired power. The trend could intensify if El Niño conditions strengthen during the southwest monsoon.

An analysis published by S&P Global, an energy market intelligence firm, on July 3 said that India’s average hydropower generation in June declined by 6.3 aGW (average gigawatt) from a year earlier, even as average electricity demand increased by 24.3 aGW. The shortfall was largely offset by a 20.7 aGW increase in coal-fired generation, while solar and wind generation rose by a combined 9.4 aGW.

The trend is not confined to India.

According to the S&P Global analysis, Japan, South Korea, Bangladesh, the Philippines and Malaysia have also witnessed lower hydropower generation. However, India and Vietnam together accounted for nearly 80% of the regional decline in hydropower generation, making them the most affected countries in Asia.

“The June decline (in hydropower generation) is consistent with the expected impact of El Niño on rainfall patterns and reservoir inflows across Asia,” the analysis said and added that hydropower generation could remain below normal if El Niño conditions persist through the summer months.

Tomorrow’s sunrise will help me in my journey; tomorrow’s cool breeze will stimulate my heart and mind and give me the leisure to reach the foot of Kailashpati – Lord Kailash. These thoughts didn’t let me sleep at night. I only sat waiting for dawn to arrive. Shreya (Hruta Durgule), who’s recently married Anish (Suyog Gorhe), is discovering the nuances of this distinction one snafu at a time.

item.title: Gandhi to Wangchuk, what history says about the success of hunger strikes in India

On Thursday night, educator and environmental activist Sonam Wangchuk ended the hunger strike he had started more than three weeks ago in Delhi. He is well-known for peaceful protests, some of them fasts, demanding statehood for Ladakh and drawing attention to the ecological fragility of the Himalaya.

This time, though, the issue was different.

In May, the question paper for the NEET-UG, the national entrance exam for medical school, leaked. In June, more than two million students were made to redo the exam – one of the largest examination frauds in recent memory.

Wangchuk began fasting in solidarity with members of the Cockroach Janata Party, a youth movement only weeks old but already nationally known. They were demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation, accountability for the leak and an overhaul of the entrance examination system itself.

India did not invent going hungry in protest, but it has clearly made the method its own. One could even fashion an alternative history of the Republic based on its major fasts – not just of marginal protests but some of the most significant confrontations between the Indian state and people.

item.title: Iran is turning into a ‘forever war’ Trump promised to avoid
item.description: The US and Iran are settling into a prolonged cycle of calibrated confrontation that lasts far longer than many currently anticipate.
item.content:encoded:
When Donald Trump returned to the White House, he promised to avoid another Middle Eastern “forever war”. After the costly experiences of Iraq and Afghanistan, that pledge resonated with an American public weary of prolonged military intervention.

For a brief moment, it appeared that this promise might be realised. The memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by the US and Iran on June 17 seemed to offer a pathway away from escalating confrontation. Markets stabilised, regional tensions eased and there was cautious optimism that Washington and Tehran had stepped back from the brink.

That optimism has proved remarkably but unsurprisingly short-lived. US military strikes have resumed and Iran has retaliated against American and its allies across the Gulf. Iran’s proxy allies, the Houthis, have declared themselves ready to close the Red Sea chokepoint at the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, which has provided an alternative transit route for some oil exports, particularly from Saudi Arabia.

Washington continues to combine military pressure with calls for renewed negotiations. But rather than representing the collapse of an isolated peace initiative, these developments may confirm the reality of grey zone conflict – where diplomacy manages war rather than ends it.

In Brazil, customers can choose between different percentages of ethanol blends or pure petrol depending on the price and usage. The tunnel collapsed on Monday after a “sudden explosion of trapped or embedded suspected methane gas within the rocks, resulting in dense smoke and toxic gases”, the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation had said.
